extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (patent attorneys, agents, in-house counsel) drafting and prosecuting AI-related patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, technology-specific guidance for identifying inventive subject matter, eliciting required technical details from inventors, drafting claims and specifications, and handling prosecution/enforcement issues for AI/ML-related patent applications across major jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting the Context
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which aspects of the AI system comprise the inventive subject matter (e.g., data selection, data preparation, computing environment/constraints, training method, inference method, architecture, application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set the stage for the disclosure interview by identifying whether the invention relates to training, inference, architecture, preprocessing, post-processing, sensors/input, application of AI, or combinations; tailor follow-up questions and claim focus accordingly. Example: pruning or reward-function tuning -> focus on training and architecture; novel use of conventional NN -> focus on inference and supporting architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying the Problem (technical challenge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the invention in terms of the technical challenge it addresses to aid 102/103 analysis and Section 101 subject-matter eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask inventors: What technical challenges did you face? Why were conventional approaches inadequate? Did you encounter unexpected problems? Use answers to craft problem/solution narrative and to show 'technological improvement' or integration into a practical application under USPTO guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying Technical Advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the technical improvements the invention provides and how those improvements are realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect quantifiable metrics (e.g., reduced processing cycles, memory utilization, power use, accuracy, latency). Improvement need not be over well-understood routine activities; it is sufficient that the functioning of a computer or other technology is improved. Claim and describe architectural aspects that demonstrate non-conventionality (e.g., compressed architectures enabling edge deployment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the System Inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what data is used as input for the system versus training, the minimum viable data, and whether particular parts of the data are dispositive to the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What data is used for training vs inference? Minimum viable type/amount? Could other data types be used? Which data elements are dispositive? How is input data manipulated before use?

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding Data Collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe how data are obtained, structured, sourced, and formatted, including sensors, local vs external sources, and batch vs online collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: How is the data collected? Are sensors/hardware involved? What is the format when collected? Volume and sources (locally generated vs third-party) can affect enablement, written description, and potential privacy/ethics considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding Preprocessing Steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain data preprocessing and feature engineering performed prior to training/inference and whether such steps are conventional or inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document cleaning, normalization, augmentation, segmentation, filtering, feature selection, geometric transformations, or other manipulations. Consider whether preprocessing is more than 'insignificant extra-solution activity' — if preprocessing contributes to improved ML performance it may support eligibility/practical application arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding Post-processing Steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe how outputs from the model are processed, calibrated, transformed or made usable for downstream tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: How is the output processed or made usable? Is calibration performed (e.g., Platt scaling)? Are outputs transformed for downstream functions? Identify devices/components performing post-processing for system-level claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the Architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture the model architecture details (off-the-shelf vs custom), high-level architecture types, layer structures, activation functions, inter-layer connections, and system/distributed deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Is the architecture off-the-shelf or custom? How does architecture relate to the solved problem? What are layer structures, activation functions, and connections? Document whether federated/distributed implementations or integrations with sensors/devices exist. Architectural specifics support written description and non-obviousness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the Training Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Document the training algorithm type (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, diffusion, etc.), training data, labeling procedures, hyperparameters, loss functions, and any automated labeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What learning algorithm is used? What training data and how labeled? Which hyperparameters were set and why? Training details affect claim drafting (training claims vs inference claims), enablement, and enforcement/detectability considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the Inference Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail inference-time behavior: how the trained model processes new input, deployment constraints, runtimes, latency, and how inference integrates with other system components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document where inference executes (edge, cloud), timing/latency constraints, input handling at inference, and any architecture/hardware enabling inference. Inference details inform claim drafting and eligibility/practical-application arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting Open-Source Component Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the invention relies on open-source components and what functionality those provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Do you use open-source models, libraries, or datasets? Which ones and what do they do? Explain modifications to off-the-shelf components to show improvement/non-conventionality and avoid enablement pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of Minimum Viable Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the minimum viable type or amount of data that could be used for the invention to function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding minimum data requirements supports enablement and written description; collect examples showing lower bounds and alternatives to demonstrate breadth without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting Hyperparameter Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Record which hyperparameters were set and why those values were chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include rationale for hyperparameter choices in specification or disclosure to support enablement and to distinguish from routine optimization; provide ranges or examples where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describing Automated Labeling or Labeling Procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe how training data is obtained or labeled, and whether automated procedures are used for labeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the labeling pipeline, quality control, annotator rules, synthetic-label generation, or auto-label algorithms; these details can be dispositive for enablement and for showing non-conventional data curation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing Whether Pre/Post-processing Is Conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether preprocessing or post-processing steps are 'well-understood, routine and conventional' or contribute to an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If preprocessing/post-processing meaningfully improves model behavior or device functioning, document the effects quantitatively; beware that merely adding conventional data prep may not confer patentable subject matter under Parker v. Flook and similar precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three Levels of Description
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide multiple levels of description in the specification (e.g., high-level overview, mid-level functional description, low-level implementation details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include conceptual descriptions, representative embodiments, and concrete implementation parameters (layer counts, parameter counts, sample datasets, training steps) to satisfy written description and enablement while supporting claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem/Solution Description
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly present the problem solved and the solution implemented, linking the technical improvement to claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use problem/solution language throughout the spec and claims to help show practical application under USPTO Step 2A Part 2 and to preempt eligibility rejections; include quantitative evidence of improvement where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting Claims for Subject Matter Eligibility (§101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft claims to demonstrate integration of any alleged judicial exception into a practical application and to recite additional elements that show technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider claim types (training, inference, architecture, problem/solution). Use system/apparatus limitations, technical constraints, specific structures, improvements to computer functioning, or specific post-processing to anchor claims. Include problem/solution wording and quantify improvements where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting Definite Claims (§112(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure claims provide clear, definite boundaries and are supported by specification to meet §112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid indefinite functional language without structure; support claim terms with examples and structure in the spec. Address representative-claim treatment (PTAB) by presenting claim-specific arguments where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting for Written Description, Enablement, Best Mode (§112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide sufficient disclosure of the invention so a person skilled in the art can recognize possession, enable replication without undue experimentation, and identify best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose datasets, model architectures, training regimes, hyperparameter choices, thresholds, and example code/weights when appropriate. Include variations and alternatives; document concrete examples to fend off §112 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training Claims (advantages and pitfalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider including claims directed to training processes or trained models, recognizing both patentability and enforcement challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training claims can help with eligibility but may be hard to detect/enforce and present split-infringement risks. Weigh strategic benefits: ability to show inventive steps in training pipeline vs practical detectability for litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference Claims (advantages and drafting focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft inference-time claims to capture deployment improvements and practical applications of trained models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize constrained inference behavior, device-specific implementations (edge/cloud), latency/resource improvements, or specific post-processing steps to strengthen §101/practical application positions and enforcement/detectability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim structural aspects of AI models (layer arrangements, novel connections, encoder/decoder structures, compressed architectures, neuromorphic or hardware accelerators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture architecture-level innovations and their functional benefits; provide detailed layer/connection descriptions, parameter relationships, or hardware arrangements in the spec to support these claims for §112 and non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem/Solution Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Include claims that explicitly tie a claimed technical solution to the technical problem and show how the solution improves a device or computer function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem/solution language can assist in practical application analysis; ensure the claim recites how the claimed elements bring about the improvement (e.g., reduced memory, increased throughput).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office Action Response Strategies for §101 Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond to patent eligibility rejections by showing that the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application or recites significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use problem/solution evidence, quantify improvements, claim specific structures, combine additional unconventional elements, and argue practical application per USPTO PEG. Prepare separate §101 arguments for representative claims when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing Mental Process and Organizing Human Behavior Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate and rebut rejections that characterize claims as mental processes or organizing human activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize concrete computer/technical implementation, sensors/data acquisition, device integration, or specific algorithmic steps performed by machines rather than purely human cognitive activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing Mathematical Concept Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Handle rejections that treat the claim as directed to mathematical formulas or abstract mental operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how the mathematical computation is applied to a technical problem in a particular machine or how it improves computer functioning; add physical or structured limitations and practical application language to claims/spec.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Specific Structures and Practical Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Include specific structures, hardware elements, or application-level details to demonstrate practical application and avoid abstract-idea characterizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim sensors, networks, edge devices, storage/processing constraints, or particular data flows; tie algorithmic elements to these structures in both claims and specification to strengthen §101 and enablement positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations of Additional Elements and Unconventional Solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that claimed additional elements and their unconventional combinations provide more than well-understood routine activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document why combinations are non-conventional and provide evidence of synergistic effects; use experimental/quantitative data where available to support inventive concept arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recent Changes Regarding Training Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of evolving practice and case law affecting the treatment, eligibility, and enforcement of training claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor USPTO, PTAB, and court decisions on training-claim eligibility and enforcement/detectability issues; adjust drafting strategy accordingly (e.g., claim both training and inference/system embodiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description and Definiteness Rejections (§112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid §112 rejections by ensuring sufficient disclosure, clear claim language, and support for terms, parameters, and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete examples (datasets, architectures, hyperparameters), define terms in the spec, and avoid overly broad claim terms unsupported by embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-Claim Treatment and PTAB Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When responding to PTAB or appeal practice, anticipate that a single method claim may be chosen as exemplary under Rule 41.37(c)(1)(iv), affecting non-method/apparatus claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present distinct arguments for different claim types and preemptively address representative-claim treatment in briefs and prosecution to avoid collateral vulnerability of non-method claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detectability and Enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how claimed steps—especially training steps—can be detected and enforced in real-world infringement scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim system/apparatus elements or inference-time behaviors that are observable; include deployment constraints, data flows, or device-based steps to improve litigability. Recognize split-infringement risks where multiple actors perform different claim steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics for AI Inventions — Safe and Effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure AI inventions are described and claimed with consideration for safety and effectiveness in their intended use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address safety measures, validation/testing results, failure modes, fallback mechanisms, and human-overrides in the specification to support practical application and regulatory/ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics for AI Inventions — Algorithmic Discrimination Protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider and document protections against algorithmic bias and discrimination in AI systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe data curation steps, fairness metrics, mitigation techniques, and testing performed to detect and reduce bias; include these in the spec as design choices and advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics for AI Inventions — Data Privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Address data privacy concerns in data collection, labeling, training, and deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document sources, consent, anonymization, differential privacy or other privacy-preserving techniques used, and any compliance considerations; these can affect enablement and commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics for AI Inventions — Notice and Explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider documenting mechanisms for user notice, explanations, and interpretability of AI outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explanation or interpretability modules, logging, or interfaces that provide reasons for AI decisions; useful for ethics, regulatory compliance, and demonstrating practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics for AI Inventions — Human Alternatives and Fallback
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe human oversight, alternatives, and fallback procedures when AI systems fail or are uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify thresholds for human intervention, fail-safe modes, and decision handoff processes in the specification to strengthen safety and practical implementation claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations for Major Jurisdictions (EPO, Japan, China, Korea, UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt drafting and prosecution strategies to jurisdiction-specific standards for patentability and inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO: emphasize 'technical character' and specific structural/technical effects; other jurisdictions have distinct approaches to AI and inventorship—review local case law and examiner guidance. Tailor claims/spec to meet regional eligibility, novelty, and inventive-step tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI Inventorship — Determine Proper Human Inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess and document human contributions to inventions assisted by AI to determine correct inventorship and avoid listing AI as an inventor where law requires natural persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify humans who conceived the inventive concept (e.g., improvement to AI system, process envisioned by a human, or human recognition of useful AI-generated output). Document roles of collaborators and AI's role as a tool; include disclosure language describing AI involvement without naming AI as inventor when required by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tips for AI-Assisted Inventions (who to list as inventor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on when human actors should be listed as inventors for AI-assisted inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List humans who conceived improvements to AI systems, who envisioned processes using AI (where AI is conventional), or who recognized the utility of AI-generated outputs. For collaborative scenarios, consider joint inventorship where multiple humans made inventive contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting AI's Role Without Assigning Inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe AI involvement in the invention disclosure/specification while complying with laws that require natural-person inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include statements in the specification about use of AI tools, datasets, and automated generation processes, but list natural persons as inventors and document their contributions to conception and reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to Proposed Legislation and Policy Changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate and adjust to proposed statutory changes (e.g., Patent Eligibility Restoration Act) that could alter eligibility analysis and PTO practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how elimination or modification of judicial exceptions might affect claim drafting strategies and the continued relevance of practical-application analysis. Maintain problem/solution claim drafting as USPTO/PTAB practice may persist despite legislative change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention Disclosure Interview Best Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use targeted disclosure questions and a clear framework to elicit the technical details necessary for drafting AI patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide inventors a disclosure form with specific questions on context, problem, technical advantages, data inputs/collection/preprocessing/post-processing, architecture, training, inference, open-source components, and improvements. Educate inventors on how to think about AI inventions to improve disclosure completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide Quantitative Evidence of Improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, collect and include measurements that quantify the claimed technical improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include reduced processing cycles, lower memory footprint, improved accuracy metrics, reduced latency, or energy savings. Quantitative evidence aids §101/practical application and non-obviousness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Drafting to Mitigate Representative Treatment Risk
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple claim types are filed, craft separate §101 and other arguments for different claim forms to avoid adverse representative-claim treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate PTAB/Examiner selection of an exemplary claim; present distinct arguments for method, apparatus, and system claims to prevent method-claim treatment from dooming non-method claims.
